structure.title: Explaining progress
structure.text: Opening chapters contrast static and dynamic societies and connect sustained progress with criticism and knowledge creation.

structure.title: A larger horizon
structure.text: Later material places humanity in cosmic history and considers future transformations through technology, institutions, and changing ideas.

people.name: Static society
people.text: A culture organised to preserve its prevailing knowledge.

people.name: Universal explainers
people.text: People considered through their capacity to create explanations.

context.title: Optimism as a claim
context.text: The authors connect solvability to knowledge rather than predicting that improvement happens automatically. Possibility and an achieved solution remain different.
context.takeaway: Ask what knowledge the proposed change requires.

context.title: Broad historical categories
context.text: Static and dynamic describe large patterns. Applying them to particular societies requires evidence beyond the usefulness of the contrast.
context.takeaway: Test the examples against the category.

passages.quote: For humans, suffering is intimately related to staticity.

notice.text: Track the move from physical possibility to institutions.
notice.why: Technical potential does not specify how people will organise it.
The cosmic perspective gives human creativity a particular argumentative role.

opening: A planet can contain everything needed for a civilisation without producing one. Materials wait; knowledge changes what can be done with them. Arjun Khemani and Logan Chipkin use that distinction to argue for a future far larger than current resources and technologies suggest. Their optimism rests on the creation of explanations and the institutions that allow criticism to improve them. The provocation is that humanity's greatest limitations may lie in ideas that can be replaced, while treating those limitations as permanent helps preserve them.
